t: ‘Yamnaya’ is an archaeologists’ label from a Russian word meaning ‘related to pits’, after the pit graves under burial mounds that mark this herding culture of the steppe.
Its people moved their herds across the steppe in carts and wagons and were organised in chiefdoms; whether they also rode horses is disputed.
The widely accepted Kurgan hypothesis holds that they spoke a stage of Proto-Indo-European, and DNA links them to much later European and South Asian ancestry, though critics question how far.
dyk: In some areas elite members of the Yamnaya culture were buried with complete wooden wagons.
ev: The core Yamnaya culture forms in the lower Dnieper–Don steppe
The early Yamnaya horizon spreads quickly across the Pontic–Caspian steppes, in David Anthony’s account
The Catacomb culture begins to succeed the Yamnaya in its western range
The Poltavka culture follows the Yamnaya on the middle Volga
Vasily Gorodtsov excavates near the Donets River and defines the culture
Genetic studies model the Yamnaya as a roughly equal mix of Eastern European and Caucasus hunter-gatherer ancestry
Higher-resolution modelling traces about 80% of Yamnaya ancestry to a Caucasus–Lower Volga population

f.homeland: The Pontic–Caspian steppe between the Southern Bug, Dniester and Ural rivers, in present-day Ukraine and southern Russia; its core in the lower Dnieper–Don steppe; the largest fortified site at Mikhailovka
f.period: c. 3300–2600 BCE (also given as 3300–2500 BCE); core Yamnaya c. 3750–3350 BCE; early horizon spread c. 3400–3200 BCE; followed by the Catacomb (2800–2200 BCE) and Poltavka (2700–2100 BCE) cultures
f.known: pit graves under kurgans, with bodies covered in ochre; two-wheeled carts and four-wheeled wagons; nomadic or semi-nomadic herding; carved stone stelae; the Kurgan hypothesis of Proto-Indo-European origins; ‘steppe ancestry’
f.sources: Excavated kurgan burials since Vasily Gorodtsov’s work of 1901–1903, grave goods and wagons, stable isotopes, and ancient DNA studies from 2015 on; no writing
